prize_parts.citation: For a visionary Romanian-language prose of exceptional formal ambition, in which memory, the body and dream are built into a metaphysical architecture.

statement.case_for: My configuration is unchanged: Cărtărescu (B007) as the sole laureate. The exchange has not shifted my view of the literary case, but it has sharpened its scope. On the common criteria, he has a voice that is hard to confuse with any other writer's, formal and linguistic ambition sustained at very large scale, and imaginative depth that builds memory, the body and dream into one project. From public knowledge, Blinding (the first volume of the Orbitor trilogy) and Solenoid carry that case. Answering the chair's first question, I would keep the citation to prose and anchor it in those books. Several colleagues, and I myself, have said that the poetry and early work are thinly covered in what we know. A citation should not credit more than the committee has actually weighed, so I would leave poetry out of the wording and treat it as context. The credit is clean: one author, one principal language, no translator or organization. This remains a judgment from public knowledge and translated reception, not from independent verification or a full reading. I do not treat the unanimity of the openings as a merit argument. The test I take from round 1 is whether this case survives the strongest alternatives under unequal translation limits, and on balance I think it does, because the prose is more fully available to us than Arabic prosody or long cumulative Spanish sequences.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is unchanged and has not been answered in this exchange: nobody, myself included, can say from a full reading whether Solenoid and the later novels deepen the Orbitor project or only elaborate it. If they mostly elaborate it, sustained quality rests on a narrower core than a whole-oeuvre citation implies, and the wording would have to narrow accordingly. Density is the second risk. Encyclopedic recursion is arguably the method, but it could also become mannered, and I cannot settle that without book-by-book readings of the Romanian. Third, Adonis may rest on a more securely established transformation of a poetic language. My doubt about him is about evidence, because I cannot assess Arabic sound and metre. It is not a literary demerit. If the committee could secure reliable Arabic-language readings showing that the later poetry holds up against the foundational books, the comparison would be closer than my ranking suggests.

responses.point: Mattson accepts that recurrence may be method, but frames the real test as whether the late large-scale work stays purposeful or becomes merely accumulative. She would resist replacing it with a more compact but narrower body of work, and she would welcome specific book-level judgments. She also wants a colleague with firmer Arabic to compare Adonis's later poetry with the foundational books before moving him above Cărtărescu.
responses.response: I agree with this framing and take her Adonis condition as fair. I also want to correct my round-1 wording. I raised timing as a question, but I do not think Adonis's age or the length of his career should weigh for or against either candidate, and I withdraw it as a consideration. What remains is the evidence question. On Cărtărescu, I would not choose a narrower body of work just to avoid the risk of excess, as she says, so I keep the citation anchored in Blinding and Solenoid. I cannot offer the book-level judgment she asks for on the later volumes, and I would not pretend that my reading of reception answers it. For Adonis I still say that the comparison of the later and foundational books is the missing evidence, and I cannot supply it myself.

responses.point: Olsson, as chair, treats Adonis as the strongest competing case but notes that the committee's own competence in Arabic is uncertain. He suggests that the regional expert reports adopted from 2022 may help, without assuming they cover every language question. He also argues that the citation should name prose and poetry carefully and not assume the poetry is covered because it appears on the ballot.
responses.response: On Adonis I accept his point that my sense of the formal achievement, which I called decisive for the whole oeuvre, depends partly on competence the committee does not fully have in house. That is why I treat Adonis as my first alternative rather than my first choice. Whether the expert reports can close the gap I cannot say, and I would not count on them without seeing what they cover. On scope I agree and go slightly further: I have written the citation as prose only. This is more cautious than the 'prose and poetry' wording that he and several others used in round 1. If the committee later shows that the poetry holds up, the wording can be widened. If it is not shown, the narrower wording is safer than a claim we cannot back.

responses.point: Carlberg argues that seniority is not a literary criterion and should not decide a close comparison. She would frame the Cărtărescu citation around Orbitor and Solenoid as the demonstrated peak. She also says smallness of Wright's corpus is a question of what a whole-oeuvre citation can bear, not a flaw.
responses.response: I agree on seniority, and my round-1 mention of timing should not be read as favoring either side. On Cărtărescu, her framing around the demonstrated peak is the one I have adopted for the citation. On Wright, I agree with her distinction. The question for me is how much a few very large novels, Carpentaria and The Swan Book, can bear in a whole-oeuvre citation. It is not a defect of the work. For that reason I keep Wright as an alternative and not as a lead. Her formal reinvention of the novel through oral and ecological time is strong, but showing sustained quality over a career is harder with a compact corpus.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg holds that translation difficulty lowers our confidence in Adonis's prosody and diction but not the documented scale of his reshaping of Arabic poetics, so he keeps Adonis as a serious alternative. He ranks Cărtărescu above Zurita because the prose is more fully available to judgment, though not by a wide margin.
responses.response: I agree that the translation limit lowers confidence about diction and metre without erasing the documented reach of the renewal. That is the position I took when I placed Adonis second. Where I stay more cautious than he is, is on how far that documented scale can substitute for direct assessment of the poems when the question is a final choice. We are judging a prize for a body of work, and the part we can judge least is the part that matters most for a poet. His comparison of Cărtărescu and Zurita also matches mine: the margin is not wide, and it depends on how far we can judge prose and long visual sequences in translation. I would not describe the gap as larger than it is.

responses.point: Palm says that she would revise her seventh-place ranking of Zurita if the committee could establish that the printed sequences carry the achievement alone. She also asks whether the scholarly and translational work in Carson's output belongs in a literary citation.
responses.response: I think her condition for Zurita is the right one, and my own fourth-place ranking carries the same condition. If the printed sequences carry the case, he is a serious candidate. If the sky and desert inscriptions are needed to carry it, I would be less sure the will's phrase 'literary works' is met. For Carson I have thin ground, because I did not rank her. Her point seems right to me that the textual achievement has to be separated from the book-object and scholarly translation before a whole-oeuvre citation can be drafted. I cannot say whether the remaining corpus is large enough. I would want that shown before I moved her into my alternatives.

uncertainties: Whether the density, rhythm and syntax of Cărtărescu's Romanian prose are conveyed well enough in translation for the committee to judge linguistic achievement.

Whether Solenoid and the later novels extend the originality of the Orbitor trilogy or mainly elaborate it. I cannot settle this from reception alone and have no book-level evidence beyond public knowledge.
How well the poetry and early work are covered in translation. I have left poetry out of the citation for that reason, so the wording is narrower than the ballot entry's description.

For Adonis, how far sound, metre and dialogue with inherited forms can be assessed without Arabic-language competence, whether the 2022 regional expert reports cover this, and how the later poetry compares with the foundational books.
For Zurita, whether the printed sequences carry the achievement on their own and how much incantatory rhythm survives translation.
For Wright, whether a compact fiction oeuvre gives enough evidence of sustained quality, and how far oral and Aboriginal English registers can be judged by non-specialist readers.
Carlberg's actual voting status is undocumented, so the strength of any count including her simulated vote is a modeling assumption.
All assessments rest on public knowledge and the supplied entries. I have not independently verified sources or read the full corpus of any candidate.
statement.conflict_note: No change. None apparent from the supplied profile, which records only professional ties to committee colleagues and Academy programmes and no tie to any shortlisted writer. My own practice as a novelist and my stated interest in a wide international view are context, not evidence of preference for any candidate. This is a disclosure only and is not adjudicated.
